english: That the Hebrews have twenty-two letters is attested also by the language of the Syrians and the Chaldeans, which is for the most part close to Hebrew. For they too have twenty-two elements with the same sound, but different characters. The Samaritans also habitually write the Law of Moses with the same number of letters, differing only in shapes and points. And it is certain that Ezra the scribe, the teacher of the Law, after the capture of Jerusalem and the restoration of the temple under Zerubbabel, discovered other letters which we now use, since up to that time the characters of the Samaritans and the Hebrews had been the same. In the book of Numbers also this same reckoning is mystically shown under the census of the Levites and priests.

And we find the name of the Lord, the Tetragrammaton, in certain Greek volumes even to this day expressed in the ancient letters. But also Psalms 36, 110, 111, 118, and 144, although they are written in different meter, are nevertheless woven together by the alphabet of the same number. And the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and his prayer, and also the Proverbs of Solomon at the end, from the place where he says, “A capable wife who can find?” (Proverbs 31:10), are reckoned by the same alphabets or sections. Moreover, there are five double letters among the Hebrews: Caph, Mem, Nun, Pe, Sade. For they are written one way through these at the beginnings and middles of words, and another way at the ends. Hence also five books are considered double by most: Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Jeremiah with Lamentations, that is, with his Lamentations. Therefore, just as there are twenty-two elements by which we write in Hebrew everything that we speak, and by their beginnings human speech is comprehended, so twenty-two volumes are reckoned, by which, as if by letters and beginnings in the teaching of God, the tender and still nursing infancy of a righteous man is instructed.
The first book among them is called Beresith, which we call Genesis.
The second, Veelle semoth, which is called Exodus.
The third, Vaiicra, that is, Leviticus.
The fourth, Vajedabber, which we call Numbers.
The fifth, Elle haddebarim, which is entitled Deuteronomy. These are the five books of Moses, which they properly call Thora, that is, the Law.
They make the second order of the Prophets, and they begin with Joshua son of Nun, who among them is called Joshua son of Nun.
Then they attach Judges, that is, the book of Judges. And they join Ruth into the same book, because her history is narrated as taking place in the days of the Judges.
The third follows, Samuel, which we call the first and second books of Kings.

The fourth is Melachim, that is, of Kings, rather than Mamlachot, that is, of Kingdoms. For it does not describe the kingdoms of many nations, but of the one Israelite people, which is contained in twelve tribes.
The fifth is Isaiah.
The sixth, Jeremiah.
The seventh, Ezekiel.
The eighth, the book of the Twelve Prophets, which among them is called There asar.
The third order holds the Writings.
And the first book begins with Job.
The second with David, whom they comprise in five sections and one volume of Psalms.
The third is Solomon, having three books: Proverbs, which they call Misle, that is, Parables.
The fourth, Ecclesiastes, that is, Coheleth.
The fifth, Song of Songs, which they entitle Sir hassirim.
The sixth is Daniel.

The seventh, Dibre hajamim, that is, Words of Days, which we can more significantly call the Chronicle of the whole divine history, which book among us is inscribed as the first and second books of Chronicles.
The eighth, Esdras, which also itself is similarly divided into two books among the Greeks and Latins.
The ninth, Esther.

And so there are together twenty-two books of the Old Law: that is, five of Moses, eight of the Prophets, and nine of the Writings. Although some write Ruth and Lamentations among the Writings, and think these books should be reckoned in their own number, and therefore there are twenty-four books of the ancient Law: whom the Apocalypse of John introduces under the number of the twenty-four elders worshiping the Lamb, and offering their crowns with faces cast down, while standing before the four living creatures, which are full of eyes before and behind—that is, looking both to the past and to the future—and crying out with unwearied voice: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Revelation 4:8).

This prologue of the Scriptures, like a helmeted beginning, can be suitable for all the books which we have translated from Hebrew into Latin, so that we may know that whatever is outside these is to be set aside among the apocryphal books. Therefore Wisdom, which is commonly inscribed as Solomon's, and the book of Jesus son of Sirach, and Judith, and Tobias, and the Shepherd, are not in the canon. I have found the first book of Maccabees in Hebrew. The second is Greek, which can also be proved from its very style. Since these things are so, I beg you, reader, not to consider my labor a reproach of the ancients. In the temple of God each one offers what he can: some offer gold, silver, and precious stones; others offer fine linen, purple, scarlet, and hyacinth. It goes well with us if we offer skins and goat hair. And yet the Apostle judges our more contemptible things more necessary. Hence also all that beauty of the tabernacle, and its distinction into each kind of the present and future Church, is covered with skins and haircloths, and the cheaper things keep off the heat of the sun and the injury of rain. Read then my Samuel and Kings: mine, I say, mine. For whatever we have learned and hold by translating more frequently and emending more carefully is ours. And when you understand what you did not know before, consider me either a translator, if you are grateful, or a paraphraser, if you are ungrateful—although I am not at all conscious to myself that I have changed anything from the original Hebrew. Certainly if you are incredulous, read the Greek and Latin codices, and compare them with these little works which we have recently emended: and wherever you see them disagree among themselves, ask any of the Hebrews to whom you should rather give credence: and if he confirms our version, I think you will not consider him a guesser, as if he had divined in the same place as I did.

But I also ask you, handmaids of Christ—you who anoint the head of the Lord reclining at table with the most precious myrrh of faith, who do not seek the Savior in the tomb, since Christ has already ascended to the Father—to set the shields of your prayers against the barking dogs who rage against me with rabid mouth and go around the city, and who think themselves learned if they disparage others. Knowing my own lowliness, I will always remember that saying: I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue (Psalm 39 [Hebrew]; 38 in the Septuagint/Vulgate numbering). I set a guard on my mouth when the sinner stood against me; I was mute and humbled, and I kept silent from good things.
title: The twenty-two Hebrew letters and the twenty-two books of the Old Testament
orientation: Jerome opens his preface by explaining that the Hebrew alphabet has twenty-two letters and that the Hebrew canon of the Old Testament likewise consists of twenty-two books, which he then lists in their Hebrew order.

english: Let a letter join those whom the priesthood joins; indeed, let not paper divide those whom the love of Christ binds. I would have written the commentaries on Hosea, Amos, Zechariah, and Malachi that you request, if my health had permitted it. You send me the support of funds; you sustain my secretaries and copyists, so that my talent may labor especially for you. And look—from every side a crowd of people with different demands presses in, as if it were fair for me to work for others while you go hungry, or as if in the account of giving and receiving I were obligated to anyone besides you. And so, broken by a long illness, so that I would not be entirely silent this year and mute before you, I have consecrated to your name a work of three days—namely, a translation of three volumes of Solomon: Proverbs, which the Hebrews call Parables and the common edition calls Proverbs; Ecclesiastes, which in Greek we can call Ecclesiastes and in Latin the Preacher; and Song of Songs, which is rendered into our language as the Song of Songs. There is also circulated the book of Panaretos, Jesus son of Sirach, and another falsely attributed book, which is inscribed as the Wisdom of Solomon. The former I found in Hebrew, not titled Ecclesiasticus as among the Latins, but Parables, joined with Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that it might match the likeness of Solomon not only in the number of books but also in the kind of their subjects. The second is nowhere among the Hebrews, and indeed its very style reeks of Greek eloquence; and some of the ancient writers affirm that this is the work of Philo the Jew. Therefore, just as the Church reads the books of Judith, Tobit, and the Maccabees but does not receive them among the canonical scriptures, so also it may read these two volumes for the edification of the people, but not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines. If indeed anyone prefers the edition of the Septuagint, he has it, emended by me long ago. For we do not forge new things in such a way as to destroy the old. And yet, when he has read very carefully, let him know that our translation is better understood, because it has not turned sour by being poured into a third vessel, but has preserved its own flavor, having been entrusted immediately from the wine-press to the purest earthenware.
title: Jerome dedicates his three-day translation of Solomon's three books to Paula and Eustochium
orientation: Jerome is writing to Paula and Eustochium, dedicating to them his translation of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs, and explaining the canonical status of Wisdom and Sirach.

english: The churches of the Lord Savior do not read the prophet Daniel according to the Septuagint; they use Theodotion's version. Why this happened, I do not know. Whether it was because the language is Aramaic and differs from our speech in certain peculiarities, and the Septuagint translators did not wish to preserve the same lines in translation; or whether the book was published under their name by someone else, I know not who, who did not know Aramaic well enough; or whether some other cause existed, I am ignorant. This one thing I can affirm: it differs greatly from the truth and was rightly rejected. One should know that Daniel especially, and Ezra, were written in Hebrew letters but in the Aramaic language, as was one passage of Jeremiah; Job also has much affinity with the Arabic tongue. Finally, when I was a young man, after reading Quintilian and Tully and the flowers of rhetoric, I shut myself up in the mill of this language. With much sweat and much time I had scarcely begun to make the panting, hissing words resound, and as if walking through a crypt I glimpsed a rare light from above, when at last I stumbled upon Daniel. I was seized with such weariness that in sudden despair I wanted to throw away all my old labor. But a certain Hebrew urged me on, and kept repeating to me in his own language, "Hard work conquers all." And so I, who had seemed to myself a mere smatterer, began again to be a student of Aramaic among the Hebrews. To confess the truth, even to this day I can read and understand Aramaic better than I can pronounce it. I mention these things to show you the difficulty of Daniel, who among the Hebrews has neither the story of Susanna, nor the hymn of the three youths, nor the fables of Bel and the dragon. These we have subjoined with a spit placed before them, which, as it were, runs them through, because they are scattered throughout the whole world, lest we seem to have cut off a large part of the volume among the unlearned. I heard a certain one of the teachers of the Jews, when he ridiculed the story of Susanna and said it was invented by some Greek or other, raise the objection that Africanus also raised against Origen: that these etymologies, "from the mastic tree, to split you" and "from the oak to saw you," derive from the Greek language. We can give our own people an understanding of this matter, so that, for example, we may say that from the holm-oak he said, "May you perish at once," and from the mastic tree, "May the angel crush you to a lentil," or "May you not perish slowly," or "O slow one, that is, pliable one, may you be led to death," or something else suited to the name of the tree. Then he mocked the three youths for having so much leisure that they played in meter in the furnace of the blazing fire and called upon all the elements in order to praise God; or what miracle or sign of divine inspiration, he asked, was it that a dragon was killed with a lump of pitch, or that the devices of the priests of Bel were detected? Were these things accomplished more by the shrewdness of a clever man than by a prophetic spirit? And when he came to Habakkuk and read repeatedly of a dish-bearer carried off from Judea to Chaldea, he asked for an example where we had read in the whole Old Testament that any of the saints had flown with a heavy body and crossed such great stretches of land in a moment of time. When one of our own, quite ready to speak, brought Ezekiel forward and said that he had been transferred from Chaldea to Judea, he ridiculed the man and showed from that very volume that Ezekiel had seen himself transported in the spirit. Finally, he argued that our Apostle too—a learned man, to be sure, who had learned the law from the Hebrews—had not dared to affirm that he was carried off in the body, but had said, "Whether in the body or out of the body, I do not know; God knows" (2 Corinthians 12:2). With these and similar arguments he was attacking the apocryphal fables in the church's book of Daniel. Leaving judgment on this matter to the reader's discretion, I give this warning: Daniel is not counted among the Prophets by the Hebrews, but among those who wrote the Writings. For all Scripture is divided by them into three parts: the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings—that is, into five, eight, and eleven books. But this is not the time to discuss that. As for what Porphyry objects against this prophet, or rather against this book, Methodius, Eusebius, and Apollinaris are witnesses, who answered his madness with many thousands of lines—whether they satisfied the curious reader, I do not know. Therefore I beg you, Paula and Eustochium, to pour out prayers for me to the Lord, that as long as I am in this little body I may write something pleasing to you, useful to the Church, worthy of posterity. For I am not much moved by the judgments of those who bark at me in the present, who slip into one side or the other either from love or from hatred.
title: Why the Church reads Daniel in Theodotion's version, and Jerome's own struggle with Aramaic
orientation: Jerome is addressing Paula and Eustochium in his preface to Daniel, explaining why the Church does not read Daniel according to the Septuagint and defending his own translation from the Hebrew.
